definition: In statistics and machine learning, a Markov blanket of a random variable is a set of variables that renders the variable conditionally independent of all other variables in the system.
details: This concept is central in probabilistic graphical models and feature selection. If a Markov blanket is minimal—meaning that no variable in it can be removed without losing this conditional independence—it is called a Markov boundary. Identifying a Markov blanket or boundary allows for efficient inference and helps isolate relevant variables for prediction or causal reasoning. The terms Markov blanket and Markov boundary were coined by Judea Pearl in 1988. A Markov blanket may be derived from the structure of a probabilistic graphical model such as a Bayesian network or Markov random field.

explainer.lead: A Markov blanket is a set of variables that makes a given variable conditionally independent of all others in the system. It matters in probabilistic graphical models and feature selection, where it isolates the variables relevant to a target.

tiers.eli5: Think of the few people whose state tells you everything you need to know about someone—once you know them, everyone else adds nothing.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use Markov blankets to prune features and speed up inference in graphical models. A pitfall is assuming a blanket is minimal; only a minimal one, called a Markov boundary, preserves the independence when any member is removed.
tiers.paperLevel: A Markov blanket of a random variable is a set of variables rendering it conditionally independent of all other variables; if no variable can be removed without losing this independence, it is a Markov boundary. The terms were coined by Judea Pearl in 1988, and a blanket may be derived from the underlying structure.

explainer.example: In a network of symptoms and diseases, the Markov blanket of a disease is the set of its parent causes, its effects, and the other causes of those effects—once known, all other nodes are irrelevant to it.
